1:
Henry lays the whole trouble at the door of Jacob's marriage to two sisters, and contrasts Rachel with the long-childless Rebekah, over whom no such quarrel arose. He finds three faults in the demand: one child would not content her, her heart was set on it inordinately, and she asked Jacob rather than God, forgetting whose heritage children are. The comparison he draws is with Hannah: Rachel envied where Hannah wept and was peremptory where Hannah was submissive, must have children and died of the second, while Hannah asked one and had four more. Jacob's rebuke he thinks just and loving, a reproof needing to be warm like a medicine, neither so hot as to scald nor so cold as to be useless. He collects the paraphrases of Jacob's question, the Chaldee making it an argument that she should have asked God and the Arabic a plea that no man can give what God denies, and reports the rabbinic saying that the keys of the clouds, the heart, the grave and the womb are entrusted to no angel.

On the giving of Bilhah all are agreed in blame but differ in emphasis. Clarke explains the custom: the handmaid was the mistress's property and so were her children, borne vicariously, which is the force of bearing upon the knees; and he glosses Rachel's phrase as being built up, the word for son coming from the word for building, a family being made of children as a house of stones. Ellicott adds that the newborn was laid first on the father's knees, whose acceptance acknowledged it, then on the mother's, and holds Rachel less excusable than Sarah, since no religious hope was involved but only vexation and envy, the most to be said being that the custom existed and may have passed for meritorious because it cost the wife something. Calvin is harshest, blaming Rachel for seeking a triumph by unlawful arts instead of fleeing to God, and Jacob for departing from a command to please a wife who was not in God's place; yet he grants that God honoured the connection with offspring, and that a union void from the beginning obtained by special privilege the honour of wedlock.

Ellicott notices that Leah says Jehovah where Rachel says Elohim, puts it partly to Rachel's half-idolatry, and observes that she uses the covenant name once she bears a child herself. The second name divides them. Gill takes the wrestlings for importunate prayer while reporting a rival rendering that makes them craftiness; Clarke prefers a root meaning to twist, quoting Parkhurst for the sense that the two families are now entwined and may yet produce the promised Seed; Ellicott defends the received rendering and denies that wrestling here means prayer, since the passage usually cited uses a different verb, and calls the victory discreditable, won by a bad custom and consisting in weaning Jacob further from the unloved Leah. Calvin weighs joining and doubling before settling on wrestlings called divine by a Hebrew idiom of excellence.

Leah answers in kind, and Calvin thinks her the greater sinner, since she had known the blessing already and despaired after a short pause, proving impatience and distrust together. Her maid's first son's name is the other puzzle. Clarke reports that it was taken for a troop, an army, a soldier or a planet, and thinks Laban's dabbling in judicial astrology makes a reference to Jupiter possible; he adds an old English Bible that rendered it simply Good luck. Calvin rejects the star outright and, guided by Jacob's later blessing, makes Leah boast rather of the number of her children. Gill hears a troop of children, or its commander. Henry and Wesley see only the rivalry, and admire the wisdom of an appointment that joins one man to one woman; Keil and Delitzsch sum it up as two wives carried away by constant jealousy over their husband.
14:
What Reuben found nobody can say for certain. Clarke reports that learned men have wasted much labour guessing — lilies, jessamine, citrons, mushrooms, figs — and rests on Hasselquist, a pupil of Linnaeus who found the mandrake ripe near Nazareth in early May, matching the wheat harvest; he adds that Greeks and Orientals held the plant to help conception, and that the Hebrew word means loves. Ellicott is confident it is the mandrake and quotes Tristram, who had often eaten the fruit without any soporific effect, so that the name rests on superstition. Henry will say only that it was some rarity pleasant to the smell, perhaps jessamine, and turns aside to observe that God provides for our delights as well as our necessities, praising the custom of blessing him on tasting a pleasant fruit. Calvin declines the botany altogether.

Reuben's age divides them. Henry and Wesley make him a little lad of five or six playing in the field; Ellicott reckons the intervals and puts him between fifteen and twenty, old enough to wander the waste alone, and adds that mandrakes would not grow on tilled land. Clarke thinks Rachel had by then engrossed Jacob's whole company, which is what she traded away. Henry sees in the bargain the advantage Jacob had taken of Esau's craving for the red pottage, and warns that there may be great sin and folly in an inordinate desire for a small thing. Calvin reads more into the scene than Moses says: a house filled with contention, the sisters perhaps not quarrelsome by nature but suffered to contend so that the punishment of polygamy might be exhibited to posterity, and Jacob torn between parties because he had broken the unity of the conjugal bond. Henry, Gill and Wesley all report Bishop Patrick's explanation, that the sisters were pressing toward the promise of a seed numerous as the stars, and of one seed in whom the nations should be blessed.

Over the fifth son the commentators fall out. Calvin says Leah boasts that her son was given as the reward of her sin and proclaims a merit instead of confessing a fault, though he allows she was moved by a wish to increase her family rather than by lust. Ellicott answers him by name: since the text says God hearkened to Leah she must have prayed, and the objection that prayer could hardly accompany such courses has little weight against untrained country women whose one anxiety was offspring — the shame being that she had to buy her husband's attention at all. The name plays on hire. On the sixth name Ellicott finds Leah unusually obscure, playing on two words that look Mesopotamian; he takes the first for the present a father adds beyond the marriage contract, finds no trace of the second, and canvasses two Syriac lexicographers and three versions, a woman's value rising in the East with each son.

Dinah is recorded, Ellicott says, because of what her story cost Simeon and Levi, and in the East a girl's birth brings no feast and no congratulation. Calvin observes that genealogies commonly pass women over except where something worth commemorating befalls them, and thinks Dinah was probably the only daughter. Clarke traces Rachel's son to the prayer her husband's rebuke had driven her to, so that faith obtained what impatience had prevented. Calvin cautions that God, with whom nothing is past or future, is subject to no forgetfulness, Scripture speaking of his remembering from the effect produced on us. Henry and Wesley draw out the double sense of the name, a reproach taken away and a son yet to be added, hesitating whether the second is inordinate desire or faith taking the mercy as an earnest of more; Calvin and Clarke read it as a prophecy answered in Benjamin. Keil and Delitzsch note that the second seven years ran out about this time.
25:
Henry admires Jacob for serving out even his second apprenticeship, since a good man does not change though he swear to his own hurt, and being deceived is no warrant for deceiving. The request to go he traces beyond homesickness: Jacob kept his affection for Canaan as the land of promise, and could not think of settling in Haran. Calvin makes the point sharper: a man whose father had lived unsettled would be laughed at for pleading mere native soil, so Jacob's claim rested on the grant. He adds Laban's injustice and the hope that time had appeased Esau, but puts the promise first. How long the service ran they dispute: Gill counts twenty years, fourteen for the wives and six for the cattle, and repeats the Jewish note that twelve children were born within seven of them while rejecting the tale that each came with a twin; Ellicott stretches the stay to thirty-four, arguing that Jacob could not travel while his children were small and that Laban's fortune needed that long to grow.

Laban's answer is all courtesy and no substance. Ellicott renders the verb I have divined, explains that it means to mutter a formula between the teeth, dismisses the derivation from serpent-omens and the guess that Laban consulted his household gods, and concludes the word had worn down to no more than I fancy. Clarke glosses it as to view attentively, to pry into. Calvin takes a middle way, that the blessing was as perceptible to Laban as if attested by prophecy, inferring from his anxiety to keep Jacob that he had proved a horn of plenty. Henry is blunter: churlish men know how to give good words when it serves their ends, and God often blesses bad men for the sake of their godly relations, though they seldom have the wit to see it or the grace to own it.

Henry notices Jacob's modesty in refusing to repeat Laban's compliment, saying only that the Lord had blessed Laban since his coming. Clarke reads that phrase as according to my footsteps and Ellicott as at my foot, prosperity following wherever Jacob went. On the colours Ellicott explains that eastern sheep are generally white and goats black or brown, distinguishes small speckles from large patches, doubts the rendering brown since the word usually means black, and notes that striped coats occur in goats but not sheep. Clarke defines the same words from a root meaning to patch, and remarks that he had seen such flocks nowhere but in Shetland, whence he had brought specimens now feeding in Middlesex.

What exactly was agreed is the hardest question, the terms and the separation seeming to contradict each other. Clarke calls the difficulty extreme, rejects one common conjecture, and solves it by observing that nothing yet belonged to Jacob, so that Laban removed not his property but everything he might later claim, leaving him a flock without one animal of the kind he was to be paid in. Calvin agrees that the compact is clearest from the separation, only cattle of one colour being left with Jacob, which left him faint hope of gain — hence his insistence that Jacob acted on an oracle and not on cunning, wishing to be enriched no other way than by God's will, while Laban caught greedily at what looked advantageous and was disappointed. Ellicott breaks from the rest twice: he corrects in time to come to to-morrow, making it a next-day audit at which any white sheep among the separated beasts would count as stolen, and argues that the sons who received them were Jacob's, Reuben being by then twenty-six. Gill and Wesley keep the plainer reading, that Laban expected a flock of one colour to cost him nothing. Keil and Delitzsch record the separation without comment; Ellicott reckons the three days' journey at thirty or forty miles.
37:
The three trees are disputed. Clarke takes the first for the white poplar, notes that the epithet means fresh rather than green since dry rods could not be peeled, leaves the second undecided between filbert and almond, and makes the third the plane, named from a root meaning naked because its bark sheds yearly — an occasion to gather Homer, Virgil and Petronius on its shade. Ellicott corrects all three from Tristram's field observation: the storax, a perfumed shrub that whitens the Galilean hills in March; the almond, no wild hazel having been found in Palestine; and the plane, the chestnut growing there only in Lebanese orchards. He adds that the vessels were the fixed troughs at the wells, the notion of gutters feeding them being modern.

Henry sets out three contrivances — the peeled rods at the watering place, the parti-coloured beasts set where the rest must look at them, and the restriction of both to the stronger season — and draws from them that a man should be master of his trade, ingenious as well as industrious, since God teaches even the husbandman discretion, remarking that strong impressions are made by the eye, with which we therefore need to make a covenant. On how it worked all agree that no miracle is required. Clarke holds the belief about impressions on the mother long established and not yet rationally accounted for, but within nature's powers, and doubts not the same trial would answer again; Ellicott calls the result physically certain; Calvin gives a physiological account and notes that Jacob chose both his season and his place. Clarke explains the strong and feeble cattle as the early and late born, and adds that English breeders would improve their stock by the same method.

Whether the whole thing was honest divides them. Henry calls it honest policy, saying the success would not justify it were there anything fraudulent in it, which he is sure there was not, since Jacob acted by divine direction. Wesley repeats his account almost word for word but withholds the verdict, referring the reader to the next chapter. Calvin faces the difficulty hardest. He refuses the defence from prior injury outright, since a man unjustly treated may not contend with equal injustice, and private vengeance would leave no place for courts; Jacob ought to have overcome evil with good, and would have been bound to had heaven not commanded otherwise. The narrative, he says, puts last what came first, relating the act before the command behind it, so that those who meet fraud with fraud may not claim Jacob as their advocate. To the objection that God cannot have prompted a deceit he answers that God is the author of no fraud when he stretches out a hand to protect his servant, and that if a human judge may sentence a thief to fourfold restitution, no less should be conceded to God.

Clarke ends by naming the chapter's four hard places — the vicarious bearing of children, the mandrakes, the terms of the bargain, the parti-coloured flocks — and thinks it better and safer to confess ignorance than to multiply conjectures under a show of learning. He allows that Laban's imposition of the elder daughter was foreign to every dictate of honesty, and that Jacob had reason, humanly speaking, to repay him in kind; but calls his talent a dangerous one, traces the habit to his mother's teaching that a good end sanctifies any means, and thinks he went beyond the divine warrant, since improving his own breed necessarily spoiled Laban's. That the record says so much against its own hero he takes for evidence of the historian's impartiality. Gill notes that surplus sheep were sold to buy camels and asses; Ellicott makes wool the likelier source of the wealth. Keil and Delitzsch record only that the feebler fell to Laban, the stronger to Jacob.
